correctness.rationale: For odd characteristic the ordered zero-sum pairs contribute 2(q-1); the nonzero-sum diagonal contributes 2q-5; the only off-diagonal solutions are related by w=z/(2z-1), whose weighted sum reduces to the cubic quadratic-character sum. Removing its three exceptional inputs yields precisely the claimed elliptic trace term in characteristic at least five, while direct degeneration resolves characteristic three. In characteristic two Frobenius maps the inverse graph additively to the inverse-square graph, yielding the stated elementary energy count. Orthogonality proves the two-frequency fourth moment. Standard elliptic Frobenius theory provides the extension recurrence; exhaustive finite-field verification across 32 examples supports but does not replace the unrestricted proof.

originality.rationale: The exact inverse-square graph energy is not a consequence of the general small-doubling energy theorem, estimates for reciprocal intervals, the classical inverse-graph fourth moment, or previously known polynomial-graph energy formulas: their objects and collision equations differ. The newly derived off-diagonal involution produces a nonsingular cubic character sum and elliptic Frobenius trace for every characteristic at least five. The known Dirichlet-character-averaged mixed fourth-moment papers concern different averages; available abstracts do not imply this two-frequency unweighted identity. Full-text gaps and unlocated equivalences remain genuine historical risks.

value.rationale: The full ordered additive energy of the canonical inverse-square rational graph is a natural invariant directly controlling a complete fourth exponential-sum moment. Its exact evaluation reveals an elliptic Frobenius trace and extension-field recurrence absent from the elementary inverse-graph case; the separate characteristic-two and characteristic-three formulas show genuine geometric degeneration. This supplies a structural, non-polynomial, exact arithmetic classification rather than a trivial bound, isolated recomputation, or arbitrary finite cutoff.
